body: It is the sibling of `NetIO`, and it declares the same two effect rows for the same reason: `NetDriver` is where a frame reaches the card, so everything above it inherits `Network.Read` and `Network.Write` and must say so. Nothing below this line performs I/O.

author: blu
body: THERE IS NO CONNECTION HERE, because UDP has none. A `UdpSocket` is four addresses and a local port -- a description of where datagrams go and what to answer to. Opening one sends nothing, closing one is not a concept, and two datagrams to the same peer are related only by the caller's intent.

author: blu
body: THE DESTINATION MAC IS THE BROADCAST ADDRESS, deliberately, and this is what `HttpFetch`'s DNS query and every TCP connection in the tree already do (`resolve-dst-mac`): the ARP cache starts empty and the gateway answers regardless. A stack that ARPed first would be more correct and would also block the first datagram behind a round trip.

author: blu
body: THE SOURCE PORT COMES BACK WITH THE DATAGRAM, because a server needs it. A client knows who it is talking to and can ignore it; a server is told who is talking to it by nothing else, and UDP carries no connection to answer along. `udp-io-reply` is the send that uses it.

author: blu
body: A frame is this socket's when it is IPv4 carrying UDP addressed to the port we sent from. The peer's source port is NOT checked: a datagram server is permitted to answer from a different port, and CoAP's separate responses are the case in the tree that does it.

author: blu
body: A server's send. The socket's configured peer port is the one a CLIENT talks to; a server answers whoever asked, which is a different port per peer and is not known until a datagram arrives.
